title: Umar Declines to Pray in the Church
text:
In 637 or 638 Jerusalem surrendered to the Arab armies after a long siege. The Patriarch Sophronius is said to have insisted on surrendering only to the caliph himself, so Umar ibn al-Khattab traveled from Medina to accept the city. Muslim and Christian traditions agree that he came simply dressed and that the city was taken without a sack.

The Egyptian Christian historian Eutychius (Said ibn Batriq), writing in the tenth century, tells what happened next. Sophronius was showing Umar around the Church of the Holy Sepulchre when the time for prayer came. The patriarch invited him to pray there. Umar declined. He explained that if he prayed inside the church, Muslims after him would claim it as a place where Umar had prayed and take it from the Christians. He went outside and prayed on the steps alone.

Eutychius adds that Umar then gave the patriarch a written document forbidding Muslims to pray on those steps in congregation. The church remained in Christian hands, and a mosque named after Umar was later built nearby.
lesson: In victory, think about what your followers will do with your example after you. Limiting your own claims can protect others for generations.
people: Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab, Patriarch Sophronius
caveat: The story is recorded about three centuries after the events and cannot be confirmed from contemporary sources.
